newsitem.title: FRANCE: French insurer Axa first-half profit leaps.
newsitem.headline: French insurer Axa first-half profit leaps.

text.p: French insurance giant Axa SA said Wednesday that profits jumped 52 percent in the first half, powered by strong performances in non-life activities and at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in the United States.

Confirming its reputation as France's most profitable insurer, Axa said net consolidated profit climbed to 1.98 billion francs ($388 million) from 1.30 billion francs ($255 million) in the corresponding 1995 period.
Sales rose 21 percent to 87.5 billion francs ($17.1 billion) while earnings per share climbed 33.1 percent to 10.57 francs ($2.07).

The showing by Axa, the lone French insurer whose balance sheet has not been hammered by exposure to a long-running property slump, beat most analysts' expectations and drove its stock higher in Paris.
"It's a very good set of numbers," one analyst said.
Chairman Claude Bebear told an analysts' meeting that he expected a good second half but that it would "be a bit optimistic" to expect it to match the first half.

Axa, which has grown from a sleepy mutual company in the 1980s into a global player that now earns less than a third of its profit in France, forecast annual earnings per share growth above 15 percent to the year 2000.

Axa's earnings were powered by a near doubling of non-life insurance profits to 610 million francs ($119.5 million) from 320 million ($62.7 million). Financial services, whose profits grew 56 percent to 618 million francs ($121 million), were another driving factor.

Especially important was the investment bank DLJ, whose contribution to profits grew 73 percent to 343 million francs ($67 million) from 198 million francs ($39 million) in the 1995 period. Axa owns 60 percent of the insurer and financial services company, Equitable Cos. Inc., which is DLJ's parent.
Australian life insurer National Mutual, acquired by Axa last year to serve as a springboard for entry into Asia, also contributed to profits.
Profits fell 10 percent in life insurance, to 504 million francs ($99 million) from 555 million francs ($109 million).
